content: The surgical treatment of ovarian tumors during pregnancy is conducted in a manner similar to that in non-pregnant women. The procedures may involve the removal of the tumor itself (enucleation), the removal of one or both ovaries (oophorectomy), or the removal of both the fallopian tube and ovary (salpingo-oophorectomy). These surgeries can be performed either through open surgery (laparotomy) or minimally invasive surgery (laparoscopy). Laparoscopic surgery offers several advantages, including a shorter hospital stay, quicker recovery to normal activities, and reduced postoperative pain. However, traditional laparoscopic techniques require the use of carbon dioxide gas to inflate the abdominal cavity, which creates space for surgical instruments by displacing the bowel. This technique, while effective, carries risks such as elevated levels of carbon dioxide in the bloodstream (hypercarbia) and the potential for accidental injury to internal organs. These complications may pose risks to the developing fetus. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of laparoscopic surgery for benign ovarian tumors during pregnancy on both maternal and fetal health, as well as its implications for healthcare resource utilization. A search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was updated on November 11, 2012, to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that compared laparoscopic surgery to open surgery (laparotomy) for the treatment of benign ovarian tumors during pregnancy. Two independent reviewers were prepared to assess the quality of the trials and extract relevant data. However, the updated search did not identify any randomized controlled trials that met the inclusion criteria. The authors concluded that while laparoscopic surgery for benign ovarian tumors during pregnancy has both potential benefits and risks, the current evidence is derived from case series studies, which are prone to bias. As a result, the findings from these studies should be interpreted with caution. The available case series provide limited information about the true benefits and risks of this surgical approach during pregnancy. To establish reliable evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of laparoscopic surgery for benign ovarian tumors in pregnant patients, randomized controlled trials are necessary.
